history.q: Which ancient Arab people carved the city of Petra into rose-red cliffs?
history.fact: The Nabataeans grew rich controlling incense and spice caravans, and carved Petra's tombs straight into the sandstone.

history.q: Which empire annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE?
history.fact: Emperor Trajan turned the kingdom into the province of Arabia Petraea, and a new road, the Via Traiana Nova, soon ran to the Red Sea.

history.q: In which year did Transjordan gain independence from Britain?
history.fact: Independence came on 25 May 1946, still celebrated as Independence Day; Emir Abdullah was proclaimed king the same day.

history.q: Which country administered Transjordan under a League of Nations mandate after the First World War?
history.fact: The British Mandate covered Palestine and Transjordan, but from 1921 Transjordan was run as a separate emirate under Abdullah.

history.q: Which royal dynasty has ruled Jordan since the founding of the emirate in 1921?
history.fact: The Hashemites trace their descent to the Prophet Muhammad through his great-grandfather Hashim, from whom the family takes its name.

history.q: Which British officer, known as 'Lawrence of Arabia', fought alongside Arab forces in the Arab Revolt of 1916-1918?
history.fact: A rock formation in Wadi Rum is nicknamed the Seven Pillars of Wisdom after Lawrence's memoir, and the 1962 film was partly shot there.

history.q: Which king ruled Jordan from 1952 until his death in 1999?
history.fact: Hussein was proclaimed king at just 16 after his father Talal abdicated, and reigned for more than 46 years.

history.q: The Roman-era city of Gerasa is known today by what name?
history.fact: Jerash is one of the best-preserved Roman provincial towns anywhere, with an oval plaza ringed by Ionic columns.

history.q: Which empire controlled the lands of modern Jordan for about four centuries until the First World War?
history.fact: The Ottomans took the region in 1516-17 and held it for roughly 400 years, until the Arab Revolt and British forces pushed them out in 1918.

history.q: The Mesha Stele, found at Dhiban in 1868, was set up by a king of which ancient kingdom?
history.fact: Carved around 840 BCE, the stele was broken soon after its discovery and pieced back together; it now stands in the Louvre.

history.q: What was Amman called in the Greco-Roman era?
history.fact: The name honoured Egypt's Ptolemy II Philadelphus; the city's Roman Theatre, seating about 6,000, still sits in downtown Amman.

history.q: In 636 CE, Arab Muslim armies decisively defeated the Byzantines at a battle named after which river?
history.fact: The Yarmouk, which today forms part of Jordan's northern border, gave its name to a battle that ended Byzantine rule over Syria.

history.q: Who became the first emir of Transjordan in 1921?
history.fact: A son of Sharif Hussein of Mecca, Abdullah ruled as emir for 25 years before becoming Jordan's first king in 1946.

history.q: Which Swiss explorer, travelling as 'Sheikh Ibrahim', became the first European in centuries to describe Petra, in 1812?
history.fact: Burckhardt said he wished to sacrifice a goat at Aaron's tomb so that his guide would lead him through the hidden city.

history.q: Which leader launched the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire in June 1916?
history.fact: Sharif Hussein, Emir of Mecca, was King Abdullah II's great-great-grandfather; Jordan's flag echoes the revolt's banner.

history.q: Amman's name comes from which Iron Age people, whose capital stood on the city's citadel hill?
history.fact: Their capital, Rabbath Ammon, stood on Jabal al-Qal'a, where the Amman Citadel now shows Roman, Byzantine and Umayyad ruins.

history.q: Gerasa (Jerash), Gadara (Umm Qais) and Philadelphia (Amman) belonged to which group of Greco-Roman cities?
history.fact: 'Decapolis' means 'ten cities'; most lay in today's Jordan and Syria, with Scythopolis just west of the Jordan River.

history.q: Ajloun Castle in northern Jordan was built in the 1180s by a commander serving which leader?
history.fact: Built by Saladin's general Izz al-Din Usama, the hilltop fort watched over the Jordan Valley and routes contested with the Crusaders.

history.q: Which crusader lord, notorious for raiding Muslim caravans, held Kerak Castle in the 1180s?
history.fact: Saladin personally executed Raynald after the Battle of Hattin in 1187, and Kerak itself surrendered to Saladin's forces in 1188.

history.q: Which British officer, nicknamed 'Abu Hunaik', commanded Jordan's Arab Legion until King Hussein dismissed him in 1956?
history.fact: 'Glubb Pasha' led the Legion from 1939; his dismissal marked the Arabisation of the army's command.

history.q: The Neolithic site of 'Ain Ghazal, on the edge of Amman, is famous for which discovery?
history.fact: Made around 9,000 years ago, the statues are among the oldest large-scale human figures ever found; some are shown at the Jordan Museum.

history.q: Bozrah, the ancient capital at today's Buseira in southern Jordan, belonged to which Iron Age kingdom?
history.fact: Edom lay south of the Dead Sea; the Hebrew Bible links its people to Esau, and its land later became Nabataean territory.

history.q: Under which king, who reigned from about 9 BCE to 40 CE, did Nabataean Petra reach its greatest splendour?
history.fact: Aretas IV called himself 'lover of his people'; many of Petra's grandest monuments, possibly including the Treasury, date from his reign.

history.q: In 1878 the Ottomans settled which refugee people among the ruins of Amman, reviving it as a village?
history.fact: Circassians from the Caucasus refounded Amman; their descendants still provide a ceremonial guard at the Royal Court.

history.q: The Battle of Mu'tah in 629, near Karak, pitted early Muslim forces against which empire?
history.fact: After three Muslim commanders fell, Khalid ibn al-Walid led the army's withdrawal and, by tradition, earned the title 'Sword of God'.

technology.q: How did the Nabataeans sustain a large city in Petra's arid valley?
choices: By channelling rainwater into rock-cut cisterns
By pumping groundwater with steam engines
By importing ice from the mountains
technology.fact: Petra's engineers built dams, terracotta pipes and cisterns to capture flash floods, enough to feed fountains and even a garden pool.

technology.q: Which mineral, harvested from vast Dead Sea evaporation ponds, makes Jordan one of the world's leading exporters?
technology.fact: Potash is a key fertiliser ingredient; the Arab Potash Company has produced it on the Dead Sea's southern shore since the 1980s.

technology.q: Which Ottoman railway through Jordan did T. E. Lawrence and Arab forces repeatedly sabotage?
technology.fact: Opened to Medina in 1908, the line ran from Damascus via Amman and Ma'an to carry pilgrims, and troops, south to the holy cities.

technology.q: How did Nabataean masons carve Petra's great façades, such as the Treasury?
choices: From the bottom up, on scaffolding
technology.fact: Masons cut a ledge at the cliff top and worked downward, so the finished upper sections never needed scaffolding.

technology.q: Petra's tombs and temples are carved directly into what kind of rock?
technology.fact: Iron and other minerals streak Petra's sandstone in pinks, reds and yellows, earning it the nickname 'Rose City'.

technology.q: Why do swimmers float so effortlessly in the Dead Sea?
choices: It is fed by hot springs
Its water is extremely salty and dense
technology.fact: The Dead Sea is roughly 34% salt, nearly ten times saltier than the ocean, so its dense water pushes bathers up like corks.

technology.q: What is the name of Jordan's national airline, founded in 1963?
technology.fact: Its hub, Queen Alia International Airport, is named after King Hussein's third wife, who died in a helicopter crash in 1977.

technology.q: Which aromatic tree resin, carried by caravans through Petra, helped make the Nabataeans rich?
technology.fact: Frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia were burned in temples across the Roman world, and Nabataean routes carried them north.

technology.q: The Tafila project in southern Jordan, opened in 2015, was the kingdom's first large farm of which energy source?
technology.fact: Tafila's 38 turbines sit on windy highlands above the Dead Sea rift and generate about 117 megawatts.

technology.q: Jordan is a major exporter of which rock, mined at Eshidiya and Al-Hasa to make fertilisers?
technology.fact: Phosphate has been mined in Jordan since the 1930s, and much of it is shipped out through the Red Sea port of Aqaba.

technology.q: Which logistics company, founded in Amman in 1982, became the first Arab-based company listed on NASDAQ?
technology.fact: Aramex was co-founded by Jordanian entrepreneur Fadi Ghandour and listed on NASDAQ in 1997; it is now headquartered in Dubai.

technology.q: Which Arabic web portal and email service, founded in Jordan in 2000, was bought by Yahoo! in 2009?
technology.fact: Maktoob, meaning 'written' in Arabic, was co-founded by Samih Toukan and Hussam Khoury and was a pioneer of Arabic webmail.

technology.q: Which canal, begun in 1959, carries irrigation water along the east side of the Jordan Valley?
technology.fact: Originally called the East Ghor Canal, it draws on the Yarmouk River and turned the valley floor into Jordan's winter vegetable garden.

technology.q: Since 2013, a pipeline of about 325 km has carried ancient groundwater to Amman from which aquifer?
technology.fact: The Disi aquifer, shared with Saudi Arabia, holds 'fossil' water that fell as rain thousands of years ago and is barely replenished.

technology.q: Jordan holds some of the world's largest deposits of which fuel resource, now burned at the Attarat power plant?
technology.fact: Oil shale is rock rich in kerogen; the Attarat plant, south-east of Amman, is one of the largest power stations built to burn it directly.

technology.q: Jordan's first satellite, the JY1-SAT CubeSat launched in 2018, was named after the radio call sign of which king?
technology.fact: King Hussein was a keen amateur radio operator who chatted with enthusiasts around the world under the call sign JY1.

technology.q: To protect Petra's Siq from flash floods, how did Nabataean engineers divert the Wadi Musa stream?
choices: With a dam and a rock-cut tunnel
Into the Dead Sea via a canal
technology.fact: Their dam sent floodwater through a tunnel around the gorge; after a deadly flood in 1963 a modern dam was built on the same spot.

technology.q: SESAME, opened near Allan in Jordan in 2017, was the Middle East's first what?
technology.fact: Built under UNESCO's auspices, SESAME's members include Cyprus, Egypt, Iran, Israel, Jordan, Pakistan, Turkey and the Palestinian Authority.

technology.q: Wadi Faynan in southern Jordan was one of the ancient world's great centres for producing which metal?
technology.fact: Huge slag heaps at Khirbat en-Nahas reveal large-scale copper smelting in the Iron Age, and the Romans later worked mines here too.

technology.q: The Umayyad bathhouse of Qusayr Amra has a dome painted with what pioneering image?
choices: A map of the heavens with zodiac figures
technology.fact: Its 8th-century dome is one of the earliest surviving depictions of the night sky on a hemispherical surface.

technology.q: Which ancient city in northern Jordan was supplied by the longest known tunnel of antiquity, explored only in the 2000s?
technology.fact: The Gadara Aqueduct's main tunnelled section runs for roughly 94 km, winding along the hills' contours like an underground canal.

technology.q: Nabataean potters were famed for what kind of fine tableware?
technology.fact: Thrown on fast wheels, the bowls had walls only a couple of millimetres thick and were painted with delicate leaves and palmettes.

technology.q: Jordan's first nuclear reactor, a research reactor inaugurated in 2016, stands at which university?
choices: Jordan University of Science and Technology
technology.fact: The 5-megawatt Jordan Research and Training Reactor near Irbid produces medical isotopes and trains the kingdom's nuclear scientists.

technology.q: Which prince founded Jordan's Royal Scientific Society in 1970?
technology.fact: Prince El Hassan, King Hussein's younger brother, was crown prince for 34 years and has long championed science and dialogue.

technology.q: Which German engineer directed construction of the Hejaz Railway?
technology.fact: 'Meissner Pasha' built the line largely with Ottoman soldiers as labour; work began in 1900 and the railhead reached Medina in 1908.

art.q: Which carved façade greets visitors at the end of Petra's narrow Siq gorge?
art.fact: Legend said pirates' gold was hidden in the stone urn at its top, and bullet marks from hopeful treasure-seekers still scar it.

art.q: In which 1989 film does Petra's Treasury hide the Holy Grail?
choices: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade
art.fact: In the film the doorway leads to a vast Grail temple; in reality it opens into a single plain rock-cut chamber.

art.q: In which 2015 film starring Matt Damon did Jordan's Wadi Rum stand in for Mars?
art.fact: Wadi Rum's red sand and towering sandstone peaks have doubled as alien worlds in many films, earning it the nickname 'Valley of the Moon'.

art.q: Downtown Amman's great hillside theatre dates from which era?
art.fact: Built in the 2nd century CE, probably under Emperor Antoninus Pius, it is still used for concerts and festivals.

art.q: Craftspeople in Petra and Aqaba make pictures of camels and deserts by layering what inside glass bottles?
art.fact: Using thin funnels and sticks, artists build up the designs grain by grain from the region's naturally coloured sands.

art.q: Which pear-shaped, fretless lute is central to classical Arabic music in Jordan?
art.fact: The oud's Arabic name, al-'ud, meaning 'the wood', is the source of the European word 'lute'.

art.q: Which line dance with rhythmic stamping is a highlight of Jordanian weddings?
art.fact: Dancers link arms or shoulders while the leader at the head of the line often twirls a handkerchief or string of beads.

art.q: During 'Petra by Night', the Siq and the Treasury are lit by what?
art.fact: Around 1,500 candles in paper bags line the route, while Bedouin music echoes off the Treasury's façade.

art.q: Traditional Bedouin tents, called 'bayt al-sha'r' ('house of hair'), are woven mainly from what?
art.fact: The black cloth tightens in the rain to become almost waterproof, while in the heat its loose weave lets breezes through.

art.q: What is the famous 6th-century Madaba Map?
choices: A wall of tiles in a mosque
A floor mosaic map in a church
art.fact: Found in St George's Church, it is the oldest surviving original map of the Holy Land and shows Jerusalem in remarkable detail.

art.q: Since 1981, which ancient Jordanian city has hosted a summer festival of culture and arts among its ruins?
art.fact: Singers, dancers and poets perform in Jerash's Roman theatres and Oval Plaza, bringing the ancient stages back to life.

art.q: Which giant Petra monument is reached by climbing roughly 800 rock-cut steps?
art.fact: Ad Deir's façade is about 47 metres wide; its name comes from crosses carved inside when it was used as a chapel in Byzantine times.

art.q: Which Jordanian film, set in the desert during the First World War, was nominated for the Best Foreign Language Film Oscar in 2016?
art.fact: Directed by Naji Abu Nowar, 'Theeb' ('Wolf') cast local Bedouin non-actors and was shot in the deserts of southern Jordan.

art.q: Jerash's monumental southern arch was built to honour the visit of which Roman emperor in 129 CE?
art.fact: The city planned to grow out to meet the arch, but the expansion never happened, so it still stands apart from the old walls.

art.q: The rababa, played by Bedouin poets in Jordan, is what kind of instrument?
art.fact: Its single horsehair string accompanies sung poetry around the coffee hearth of a Bedouin tent.

art.q: Which Amman mosque, completed in 1989, is known for its great blue mosaic dome?
art.fact: King Hussein built it in memory of his grandfather; the dome is ringed with Qur'anic verses.

art.q: Which English poet described Petra as 'a rose-red city half as old as time'?
art.fact: Burgon won Oxford's Newdigate Prize for the poem in 1845, even though he had never actually seen Petra.

art.q: Wadi Rum stood in for the desert moon Jedha in which 2016 Star Wars film?
art.fact: Wadi Rum returned to the saga in 'The Rise of Skywalker' (2019), this time as the desert planet Pasaana.

art.q: The Umayyad fresco known as the 'Painting of the Six Kings' survives in which desert castle?
art.fact: The fresco shows rulers, probably including Byzantine, Persian and Visigothic kings, seemingly paying homage to the caliph.

art.q: The carved façade of Qasr Mshatta, an Umayyad palace near Amman, is now displayed in which city?
art.fact: Ottoman Sultan Abdul Hamid II gave the façade to Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1903; it now stands in Berlin's Pergamon Museum.

art.q: The Nabataeans often represented their chief god, Dushara, as what?
art.fact: These sacred stones, called betyls, are carved in niches all over Petra, a few with stylised eyes and a nose.

art.q: Which poet, known by the pen name 'Arar', is celebrated as Jordan's national poet?
art.fact: Born in Irbid in 1899, Arar wrote witty verse championing ordinary people; his son Wasfi al-Tal later became prime minister.

art.q: Which Amman-born novelist wrote the 'Cities of Salt' quintet about the coming of oil to Arabia?
art.fact: Munif, born in 1933 to a Saudi father and an Iraqi mother, was also a petroleum economist, giving his novels an insider's eye.

art.q: Which royal painter and art historian founded the society that opened the Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts in 1980?
art.fact: Princess Wijdan is a pioneer of abstract Arabic calligraphic art; the gallery specialises in modern art from the developing world.

art.q: Which UNESCO-listed site south of Madaba has an 8th-century church mosaic depicting cities of the Holy Land?
art.fact: The floor of the Church of St Stephen at Umm ar-Rasas, ancient Kastron Mefa'a, was laid under early Islamic rule.

politics.q: Who succeeded King Hussein on the Jordanian throne in 1999?
politics.fact: Abdullah II, born in 1962, is King Hussein's eldest son; he served as an army officer and special forces commander before becoming king.

politics.q: Which city is Jordan's capital and seat of government?
politics.fact: Amman began as a small village refounded in the 1870s; today it is home to around four million people.

politics.q: What form of government does Jordan have?
politics.fact: The king is head of state and appoints the prime minister, while a two-chamber National Assembly passes laws.

politics.q: Jordan's parliament has two chambers: the elected House of Representatives and which appointed chamber?
politics.fact: Senators are appointed by the king, and the constitution says the Senate may be no more than half the size of the House.

politics.q: Which queen, married to King Abdullah II, is known worldwide for her advocacy of education?
politics.fact: Rania Al-Yassin was born in Kuwait in 1970, studied business in Cairo and became queen when Abdullah II took the throne in 1999.

politics.q: Which American-born queen was married to King Hussein from 1978 until his death?
politics.fact: Born Lisa Halaby, she was in Princeton University's first co-educational class, graduating in architecture and urban planning.

politics.q: Jordan, then Transjordan, was a founding member of which organisation in 1945?
politics.fact: The Arab League was founded in Cairo in March 1945 by Egypt, Iraq, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Transjordan, with Yemen joining soon after.

politics.q: Under Jordan's constitution, who appoints the prime minister?
politics.fact: The prime minister and cabinet are responsible to the House of Representatives, which can bring down a government with a vote of no confidence.

politics.q: What title did Abdullah I hold as ruler of Transjordan from 1921 until 1946?
politics.fact: Abdullah took the title of king at independence in 1946, and the country became the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in 1949.

politics.q: Who was named Crown Prince of Jordan in July 2009?
politics.fact: Born in 1994, Crown Prince Hussein is the eldest son of King Abdullah II and Queen Rania and studied history at Georgetown University.

politics.q: In which year did Jordan and Israel sign their peace treaty at the Wadi Araba crossing?
politics.fact: Signed on 26 October 1994, it made Jordan the second Arab state, after Egypt, to sign a peace treaty with Israel.

politics.q: Which king reigned for only about a year (1951-1952) yet gave Jordan the constitution still in force?
politics.fact: Talal's 1952 constitution made the cabinet answerable to parliament; he abdicated for health reasons and lived in Istanbul until 1972.

politics.q: In which year was Jordan admitted to the United Nations?
politics.fact: Jordan first applied in 1946 but was admitted only in December 1955, in a package deal that let 16 countries join at once.

politics.q: In which city was King Abdullah I assassinated in July 1951?
politics.fact: He was shot at the Al-Aqsa Mosque; his teenage grandson Hussein was beside him, and a medal on Hussein's uniform is said to have deflected a bullet.

politics.q: The seven points of the white star on Jordan's flag are said to stand for what?
choices: The seven verses of the Qur'an's opening sura
politics.fact: The star sits in a red triangle; the black, white and green stripes recall the Abbasid, Umayyad and Fatimid caliphates.

politics.q: How many governorates is Jordan divided into?
politics.fact: Amman Governorate alone holds around two-fifths of the population; the largest by area is Ma'an, in the south.

politics.q: Jordan's army still carries which name, inherited from the Arab Legion?
politics.fact: The Arab Legion was set up under British officers in the early 1920s and was fully placed under Jordanian command in 1956.

politics.q: King Abdullah II's mother, Princess Muna al-Hussein, was born in which country?
politics.fact: Born Antoinette Gardiner in England, she married King Hussein in 1961; a Jordanian nursing college bears her name.

politics.q: In 1958 Jordan briefly united with which other Hashemite kingdom in the 'Arab Federation'?
politics.fact: Formed in February 1958 between the two Hashemite kingdoms, the federation ended within months when Iraq's monarchy was overthrown that July.

politics.q: In which year did Jordanian women gain the right to vote and stand in national elections?
politics.fact: Because no general election was held between 1967 and 1989, women first voted in a nationwide parliamentary election in 1989.

politics.q: Who in 1993 became the first woman elected to Jordan's House of Representatives?
politics.fact: Toujan Faisal, a former television presenter, won one of the seats reserved for Circassian and Chechen candidates in Amman.

politics.q: Jordan's appointed Senate is known in Arabic as Majlis al-A'yan. What does this mean?
politics.fact: The elected lower house is the Majlis al-Nuwwab, and together the two chambers form the National Assembly, Majlis al-Umma.

politics.q: Jordan's Constitutional Court was established in which year, following constitutional amendments in 2011?
politics.fact: The court rules on whether laws and regulations comply with the constitution, a role previously left to other bodies.

politics.q: Prince Hassan bin Talal served as Jordan's crown prince from 1965 until which year?
politics.fact: Weeks before his death in February 1999, King Hussein named his eldest son Abdullah as crown prince in Hassan's place.

politics.q: Transjordan's first constitutional document, issued in 1928 under the British mandate, was known as what?
politics.fact: The Organic Law created a Legislative Council and was replaced in 1947 by a constitution for the newly independent kingdom.

current-affairs.q: In June 2025, Jordan's men's football team qualified for its first ever FIFA World Cup. Which edition?
current-affairs.fact: Jordan sealed its place with a 3-0 away win over Oman on 5 June 2025, setting off celebrations across the kingdom.

current-affairs.q: Jordan reached its first AFC Asian Cup final in February 2024. Which host nation beat them in it?
current-affairs.fact: On the way, Jordan stunned South Korea 2-0 in the semi-final; Qatar won the final 3-1 at Lusail Stadium.

current-affairs.q: In June 2023, Crown Prince Hussein married Rajwa Al Saif, an architect from which country?
current-affairs.fact: Rajwa studied architecture in the United States and became Princess Rajwa Al Hussein on her marriage.

current-affairs.q: In 2021 Jordan celebrated the centenary of which event?
choices: The founding of the Emirate of Transjordan
current-affairs.fact: Abdullah I established the emirate in Amman in April 1921, laying the foundations of today's Hashemite Kingdom.

current-affairs.q: In 2022, which Jordanian national dish was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list?
current-affairs.fact: Mansaf is lamb cooked in a sauce of fermented dried yogurt called jameed, served on rice from a shared platter at weddings and feasts.

current-affairs.q: Which 2021 film by Denis Villeneuve used Wadi Rum for scenes on the desert planet Arrakis?
current-affairs.fact: Its sequel, 'Dune: Part Two' (2024), also returned to Jordan's deserts for filming.

current-affairs.q: In 2024 Jordan marked King Abdullah II's Silver Jubilee. How many years had he been on the throne?
current-affairs.fact: He became king on 7 February 1999, on the death of his father, King Hussein.

current-affairs.q: At the Paris 2024 Olympics, Saleh Elsharabaty won silver for Jordan in which sport?
current-affairs.fact: It was his second Olympic silver after Tokyo 2020; Jordan's first Olympic gold, at Rio 2016, also came in taekwondo.

current-affairs.q: In 2024, archaeologists announced a tomb holding a dozen skeletons beneath which Petra monument?
current-affairs.fact: The hidden chambers lie under the plaza in front of the Treasury and also held bronze, iron and pottery artefacts.

current-affairs.q: In August 2024, Crown Prince Hussein and Princess Rajwa welcomed their first child. What is her name?
current-affairs.fact: Princess Iman bint Hussein shares her name with her aunt, King Abdullah II's elder daughter.

current-affairs.q: Which Jordanian hill town, known for its golden limestone Ottoman-era houses, joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Inscribed as 'the Place of Tolerance and Urban Hospitality', As-Salt flourished as a merchant hub in the late Ottoman period.

current-affairs.q: Jordan's parliamentary election of September 2024 was the first in which a large share of seats was filled through what?
current-affairs.fact: Under the 2022 election law, 41 of the 138 House seats went to national party lists, a share set to grow in later elections.

current-affairs.q: Whom did King Abdullah II appoint as prime minister in September 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Jafar Hassan, an economist who had headed the king's office, succeeded Bisher Al-Khasawneh.

current-affairs.q: In 2021 Amman began operating what kind of public transport system, running in dedicated lanes?
current-affairs.fact: Amman's BRT buses use their own lanes along busy corridors, a new way to beat traffic in the hilly, car-dependent capital.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, UNESCO inscribed which art on its intangible heritage list in a joint file from 16 Arab states, including Jordan?
current-affairs.fact: The listing celebrates the knowledge and skills of writing Arabic script in flowing, artistic forms.

current-affairs.q: In 2019, which supernatural teen drama filmed in Petra and Amman became Netflix's first Arabic-language original series?
current-affairs.fact: The series follows Jordanian high-school students whose school trip to Petra unleashes a jinn.

current-affairs.q: At the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, Jordan's Abdel Rahman Almasatfa won bronze in which sport, then making its Olympic debut?
current-affairs.fact: He took bronze in the men's 67 kg kumite; Jordan also won a silver in taekwondo at the same Games.

current-affairs.q: Petra welcomed more than how many visitors in 2019, a record year for the site?
current-affairs.fact: Most visitors enter through the Siq, a winding gorge about 1.2 km long with walls up to 80 metres high.

current-affairs.q: Who was appointed Jordan's prime minister in October 2020?
current-affairs.fact: A career diplomat, Al-Khasawneh had served as an ambassador abroad and as an adviser at the Royal Hashemite Court.

current-affairs.q: Which Moroccan coach led Jordan to the AFC Asian Cup final in 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Ammouta had won the CAF Champions League with Wydad Casablanca before taking the Jordan job in 2023.

current-affairs.q: In 2019 SESAME, the synchrotron near Allan, became the world's first accelerator facility powered by what?
current-affairs.fact: A dedicated solar power plant supplies its electricity, easing the energy bills of a lab shared by eight Middle Eastern members.

current-affairs.q: Which 2021 Netflix drama, set at an elite girls' school in Amman, was created by Tima Shomali?
current-affairs.fact: The series follows a bullied student's plan for revenge and was made with a largely female cast and crew.

current-affairs.q: Which northern Jordanian city was named Arab Capital of Culture for 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Irbid, home to Yarmouk University, hosted a year of exhibitions, concerts and literary events.

current-affairs.q: Which dark basalt town near the Syrian border was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Umm el-Jimal's black basalt houses, churches and reservoirs span Roman, Byzantine and early Islamic times.

current-affairs.q: At which Amman palace did Crown Prince Hussein and Rajwa Al Saif marry in June 2023?
current-affairs.fact: After the ceremony, a motorcade carried the couple through Amman's streets to their wedding reception.

general.q: The Dead Sea shore is the lowest point on dry land on Earth. Roughly how far below sea level does it lie?
general.fact: Its level is falling by around a metre a year, as water from the Jordan River is diverted for farms and cities.

general.q: What is Jordan's currency?
general.fact: The Jordanian dinar is divided into 1,000 fils and has been pegged to the US dollar since 1995.

general.q: Jordan's only stretch of coastline, at Aqaba, lies on which sea?
general.fact: Jordan's coast is only about 26 km long, but its coral reefs make Aqaba a favourite with divers.

general.q: Which blend of wild thyme, sumac and sesame do Jordanians enjoy with bread and olive oil?
general.fact: Warm bread dipped first in olive oil and then in za'atar is a breakfast staple across Jordan and the Levant.

general.q: What is Jordan's official language?
general.fact: Most Jordanians speak a Levantine dialect of Arabic, Bedouin communities keep distinctive dialects of their own, and English is widely taught.

general.q: Which UNESCO-listed desert in southern Jordan is famed for red sands, sandstone mountains and Bedouin camps?
general.fact: Wadi Rum also holds thousands of ancient rock carvings and inscriptions, part of why it became a World Heritage Site in 2011.

general.q: Which Jordanian site was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007?
general.fact: Petra shares the title with Machu Picchu, the Colosseum, the Taj Mahal, the Great Wall, Chichén Itzá and Christ the Redeemer.

general.q: From which mountain near Madaba is Moses said to have viewed the Promised Land?
general.fact: On clear days the summit looks out over the Dead Sea and Jordan Valley; Pope John Paul II visited in 2000.

general.q: What is the red-and-white chequered headscarf widely worn by Jordanian men called?
general.fact: Worn by soldiers and the famous Desert Patrol, the red-and-white shemagh has become a symbol of Jordan.

general.q: Al-Maghtas, 'Bethany Beyond the Jordan', is revered as the site of which event?
general.fact: UNESCO listed the site in 2015; archaeologists have found Roman and Byzantine churches, baptismal pools and hermit caves there.

general.q: Which of these countries does NOT share a border with Jordan?
general.fact: Jordan's longest land border is with Saudi Arabia, running along its south and east.

general.q: Which nature reserve, stretching from mountain heights down to the Wadi Araba desert, is Jordan's largest?
general.fact: Dana spans four bio-geographical zones, and the restored stone village of Dana on its rim welcomes hikers.

general.q: Which reserve, whose river canyon drains into the Dead Sea, is known as the lowest nature reserve on Earth?
general.fact: Hikers wade and swim up the Mujib's sandstone gorge, while Nubian ibex pick their way along the cliffs above.

general.q: What is Jordan's national flower?
general.fact: The black iris blooms briefly in spring; its deep purple petals look almost black.

general.q: The Nabataean script used at Petra evolved into which modern alphabet?
general.fact: Inscriptions from Jordan and the wider region show Nabataean letters gradually turning into early Arabic script.

general.q: Which dish of rice, vegetables and meat is named for being flipped upside down onto a platter before serving?
general.fact: 'Maqluba' means 'upside down' in Arabic; cooks turn the pot over at the table, hoping the layered rice holds its shape.

general.q: Which ancient route through the highlands links Madaba, Karak, Shobak and Petra?
general.fact: Mentioned in the Book of Numbers, it was later used by Nabataean caravans and by pilgrims heading to Mecca.

general.q: Which is Jordan's oldest university, founded in Amman in 1962?
general.fact: It began with a single faculty of arts and now teaches tens of thousands of students.

general.q: The Jordan Rally, with stages near the Dead Sea, was a round of which series in 2008 and 2010-2011?
general.fact: Its service park sat on the Dead Sea shore, making it the lowest-lying event in world motorsport.

general.q: Which peak near the Saudi border is Jordan's highest mountain, at about 1,850 metres?
general.fact: Nearby Jabal Rum, at about 1,734 metres, was long thought to be the highest; from Umm al-Dami you can glimpse the Red Sea.

general.q: Which small rose-pink bird is Jordan's national bird?
general.fact: The male's rosy plumage echoes the colour of Petra's sandstone, where it is often spotted.

general.q: The Dead Sea lies on a fault where which two tectonic plates slide past each other?
general.fact: This Dead Sea Transform runs from the Red Sea to Turkey; movement along it has shifted the land by about 105 km over millions of years.

general.q: Which cargo ship was deliberately sunk off Aqaba in 1985 to become a famous dive site?
general.fact: The fire-damaged Lebanese freighter was scuttled at the initiative of Prince Abdullah, now King Abdullah II, a keen diver.

general.q: Shobak Castle, built by King Baldwin I of Jerusalem in 1115, was originally called what?
general.fact: Its Latin name, Mons Regalis, means 'Royal Mountain'; it fell to Saladin in 1189 after a long siege.

general.q: Which basalt fortress in the eastern desert did T. E. Lawrence use as his base in the winter of 1917-18?
general.fact: Lawrence lodged in a room above the gatehouse; the fort stands by the Azraq oasis, long a key stop on desert caravan routes.
